title: DraftSmith powered by Excalidraw
pitch: An Excalidraw fork that declares eight tools on document.modelContext. Any agent - ours, ChatGPT, or one that's never heard of it, discovers the vocabulary and edits the live canvas. No screenshots!!

No screenshots!! Like Comment Story Updates Title End Draftsmith (powered by Excalidraw) Live: https://nice-field-0f080db0f.7.azurestaticapps.net Inspiration Every architecture conversation we've had starts on a whiteboard and ends with someone taking a photo of it. If you actually want to keep the diagram, somebody has to sit down and redraw it, and that's the point where you stop thinking about the system and start nudging boxes around to fit one extra service in. We'd already tried the usual escapes. Mermaid and similar tools hand you a rendered picture; change one word and the layout reshuffles under you, and you can't just grab a box and move it. Image models produce something diagram-shaped that can't be edited at all. Agents that drive a canvas by clicking are guessing coordinates off screenshots, and the results look like it. Two things made us think this was worth a weekend. The first is that Excalidraw already stores the right thing. A scene is real data: elements, and arrows that stay bound to the shapes they connect. If an agent could write that scene directly, you'd get a diagram you can keep working in instead of a picture of one. The second is WebMCP. Normally the backend owns the tool list and one bespoke agent loop calls it. WebMCP flips that around: the page declares what it can do, and any agent the browser trusts can discover and call those tools. We wanted to see whether that actually holds up on something hard, and a canvas is about as hard as it gets - it's stateful, it's spatial, and it's basically opaque to an agent that can only click. Somewhere in there we also decided that a diagram handed over with no commentary isn't much use. So the agent should be able to explain what it drew, not just draw it. What it does Draftsmith is Excalidraw with an agent living inside it. Describe a system, get a diagram. "Draw a 3-tier architecture with a load balancer, two app servers and a database" comes back laid out in one turn: ranked into tiers, ordered to reduce arrow crossings, with long arrows routed around whatever sits between their endpoints. Arrows use Excalidraw's native binding, so they snap to shape edges and follow the boxes when you drag them. Nothing about it is an export - you can keep editing by hand, or keep asking. Talk to it while it draws. Voice mode runs hands-free over a single socket. It listens continuously, answers out loud, asks follow-up questions when your request is vague, and pushes back if the design looks off. You can talk over it to cut it off. When a question needs actual thought ("40M events a day, Postgres is melting - shard, CQRS, or a queue?") it says "let me think about that for a second" out loud and hands that one turn to a stronger model, rather than running the whole conversation slowly for the handful of turns that need it. Point at things. Select shapes on the canvas and they show up as pills above the composer, the same way you'd select code before asking your editor about it. "Make this blue" restyles that box and nothing else. "Connect these" binds them in the order listed. No guessing from labels. Ask to be taught. "Walk me through this" starts a spoken walkthrough with a Tutor cursor tracing the canvas, moving to each element as it's explained and panning off-screen ones into view. The finished lesson goes into the chat history, so a follow-up like "why is there a load balancer?" already has it as context. Teaching is a tool rather than a UI mode, which means "draw a 3-tier architecture and then explain it to me" draws it, binds it and teaches it in a single turn. The canvas is a WebMCP tool provider. Eight tools ( get_scene , create_diagram , add_shape , add_text , bind_arrow , set_style , remove_element , teach_diagram ) are declared to the browser, so an agent that knows nothing about our code can still drive the canvas. The panel header shows WebMCP · native · 8 tools or · shim · , and clicking the badge opens the live manifest. That was partly so we could debug it without devtools, and partly so a demo can't quietly imply native support it doesn't have. How we built it It's a fork of Excalidraw with the agent added, but we didn't vendor upstream. setup.sh clones a pinned Excalidraw commit and copies our files in. The repo stays at roughly the 6k lines that are actually ours, and our diff stays readable. The browser owns the tool definitions. app/ai-agent/webmcp/descriptors.ts is the only source of truth for the tool surface, and it lives in the browser because that's where WebMCP expects it - the page is the provider, so the declarations belong next to the code that runs them. The backend gets the list with every request. It carries its own copy, but that's a clearly labelled fallback for clients too old to send one. Our own agents are WebMCP clients. The sidebar and the voice agent both go through callTool exactly like a third party would. This was deliberate. If we'd registered the tools and then kept calling the canvas directly, the published path would have been exercised by nobody and would have rotted within days. As it stands, if the WebMCP surface breaks, the product breaks with it, and we find out immediately. The model does semantics, code does geometry. create_diagram takes an entire graph, and app/ai-agent/layout.ts runs a layered (Sugiyama) pipeline over it: break cycles, assign layers, insert dummy nodes so a long edge reserves a corridor in each layer it crosses, order within layers to cut crossings, then assign coordinates. Those dummy corridors turn into real bend points on the arrow, and since Excalidraw keeps bend points on a bound arrow, the routing survives without losing the bindings. Spatial invariants live in the tool layer. add_shape finds a non-overlapping position before it creates anything, searching outward on a grid, and reports back where the box actually ended up. Colour is assigned per layer instead of per box, so a tier comes out consistent without the model having to think about it. House style - rounded corners, hachure fill, label colour matched to the border - is set in code, so it holds regardless of what the model asks for. Voice is one socket, speech to speech. Mic audio goes up; spoken audio and tool calls come back down, over the Azure OpenAI Realtime API. One model hears audio and replies with both audio and function calls on the same stream, so there's no STT → LLM → TTS chain to keep in sync. The server proxies the socket instead of minting a client token. That keeps the key out of the browser, and because only the server sends session.update , a tampered client can't swap the instructions or widen the tool list. It can talk and listen, and that's it. The lesson is data, not prose. The scene goes to the backend, which runs a teaching prompt with one forced tool call that returns { intro, segments: [{ elementIds, narration }], closing } . Since every chunk of narration names the elements it's about, the frontend can point the cursor at exactly those elements for exactly as long as that chunk is playing. We treat the output as untrusted: schema-checked, then every element id verified against the real scene, with invented ids dropped and a lesson about nothing real rejected outright. Narration uses the browser's own speechSynthesis , so it needs no key and no audio leaves the machine. The tracing cursor isn't custom drawing either - "Tutor" is a synthetic entry in Excalidraw's collaborators map, the same code that renders a teammate's pointer, so it pans and zooms with the scene for free. No server-side session state. Each POST /api/chat is one model turn. It returns either final text or the tool calls to run; the browser runs them against the live editor and posts again. The server is a pure function of the history it's given, so it restarts cleanly, scales without stickiness, and holds the only copy of the credentials. Azure OpenAI and Anthropic sit behind one interface and are selectable per request. It's deployed as two halves on Azure, because they need different things. The editor is a static bundle on Static Web Apps. The backend has to hold a WebSocket open for the length of a voice session, which rules out serverless. Challenges we ran into Arrows went straight through the boxes. The bindings were fine - correct element ids on both ends - but the geometry wasn't, and it took a while to see why. Excalidraw derives an arrow's fixedPoint from the endpoint you seed it with: [(px - box.x) / box.width, …] . Seed an arrow centre to centre and you've recorded [0.5, 0.5] , which literally means "anchor at the centre of this shape." Seeding between the two outlines gives you bottom-centre and top-centre instead.
